source.title: Assessing Deceleration Performance: Methodological and Practical Considerations

paper.citation: Harper, D. J., Philipp, N. M., Eriksrud, O., Jones, P. A., Graham-Smith, P., & Dos'Santos, T. (2026). Assessing deceleration performance: Methodological and practical considerations. Sports Medicine, 56(1), 1–22. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-025-02339-7
paper.abstract: What methodological and practical issues should practitioners consider when assessing deceleration in field-based environments? Narrative methodological review; no newly recruited participant sample. Context: Athletes in multidirectional sports, with discussion spanning performance, rehabilitation, and injury-risk applications. Transfer: Directly relevant to collegiate American football as a multidirectional collision sport, but device-specific evidence must be checked against the exact hardware, task, and processing pipeline used locally. Narrative review and practical-considerations article comparing change-of-direction and acceleration–deceleration tests and radar, laser, video, GNSS, IMU, and motorized-resistance technologies. It does not report a systematic search, study-selection flow, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or meta-analysis; recommendations therefore synthesize a heterogeneous literature rather than estimate pooled effects. Protocol and metric definitions are organized around the velocity–time profile and early/late deceleration phases.
paper.tldr: This article provides an applied framework for selecting deceleration tests, technologies, metrics, and technique observations in multidirectional-sport athletes. Reported laser-derived deceleration metrics showed moderate-to-excellent relative reliability in selected tests, but coefficients of variation of 11–38% for several metrics could limit detection of small changes. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Narrative review and practical-considerations article comparing change-of-direction and acceleration–deceleration tests and radar, laser, video, GNSS, IMU, and motorized-resistance technologies. It does not report a systematic search, study-selection flow, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or meta-analysis; recommendations therefore synthesize a heterogeneous literature rather than estimate pooled effects. Protocol and metric definitions are organized around the velocity–time profile and early/late deceleration phases.
paper.findings: Reported laser-derived deceleration metrics showed moderate-to-excellent relative reliability in selected tests, but coefficients of variation of 11–38% for several metrics could limit detection of small changes. A 1080 Sprint protocol in a 30-m acceleration–deceleration test showed inter-session CVs of 5.3–7.1% and ICCs of 0.92–0.97 for selected metrics, while shorter-distance and other-device validity remained unresolved. Cross-system comparison is discouraged because filtering differs among devices and software; repeated monitoring should use the same device and processing application. Ratio metrics can change through either component and compound measurement error, so their component measures should also be monitored.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review without a reproducible systematic-review method; absence-of-evidence statements and practice priorities should not be read as pooled causal conclusions. Reliability is protocol-, device-, algorithm-, operator-, and population-specific. Associations between movement-quality scores and knee loading do not establish prospective injury prediction or prove that modifying the score reduces injury. The review's broad multidisciplinary recommendation is expert synthesis, not a tested implementation effect.
paper.practicalImplications: For collegiate American football, define the assessment task and decision first, then choose a device and metric with acceptable same-protocol error. Keep raw component metrics alongside ratios, standardize filtering and operators, and avoid comparing values across technologies as though they are interchangeable.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. For collegiate American football, define the assessment task and decision first, then choose a device and metric with acceptable same-protocol error. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
